title: The Deal That Wasn't: Trump Says Iran War Is Over — Tehran, the IRGC, and the Strait of Hormuz Say Otherwise
narrative:
On June 11–12, 2026, President Donald Trump made a sequence of overlapping public statements claiming the war with Iran was effectively over. At a virtual Georgia rally on June 11, Trump said 'we ended the war with Iran today … they have agreed never to have a nuclear weapon.' On June 12, he posted on Truth Social that 'discussions and final points have been … approved by all parties involved, including the United States, Israel and Gulf states.' Asked by reporters whether Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei personally approved the deal, Trump said 'I understand the answer is yes.' He cancelled strikes he had announced 'VERY HARD TONIGHT' hours earlier, citing progress, and added that the 'deal' would reopen the Strait of Hormuz 'very soon, maybe over the weekend in Europe' with Vice President JD Vance flying out for the signing. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif told reporters a 'final, agreed upon text of the peace deal has been reached.' Al Arabiya reported Iran conveyed approval of a draft via Qatari mediators. The White House described a 'five-point performance-based plan.'

Within 24 hours, every load-bearing element of that framing was contradicted by the people whose signature the deal would need to be real.
telemetry: Trump at virtual GA rally, June 11 2026: 'We ended the war with Iran today … they have agreed never to have a nuclear weapon'

analysis:
A presidential declaration that a war is over is one of the strongest possible public claims a head of state can make, because it implies a chain of authoritative actions: a counter-party has agreed, terms have been set, a signing is imminent. Each of those links is checkable against the counter-party's own public statements. Iran's foreign ministry has not hedged. It has flatly contradicted the claim. Esmaeil Baqaei said 'we have not reached a final conclusion' and accused Washington of 'new demands' and 'changing positions.' Abbas Araghchi said an MOU is 'closer' but 'pending its finalization' — the same qualification that the White House omitted in its rally script. The IRGC and Iranian Army issued separate statements vowing a 'crushing' response to US strikes, claimed attacks on three US bases, and said they engaged an F-16. Iran's Hormuz oversight body said the strait 'will be closed until further notice.' The 24-hour gap between Trump's 'we ended the war' and the IRGC's 'crushing response' is the story.

Netanyahu's office gave the central kill shot. It said Israel is 'not a party to the MOU' — three words that wipe out Trump's Truth Social line that the deal was 'approved by all parties involved, including the United States, Israel and Gulf states.' The Israeli government is on the record disclaiming the deal Trump claimed Israel approved. There is no way to reconcile these two statements. One of them is wrong. The party whose signature is supposedly on the document is the party saying no signature exists.

The Vance trip is the visual centerpiece. A vice president flying to Europe to 'attend a signing' of a memorandum that the other signer's foreign ministry has not finalised is not diplomacy. It is a photo op staged against a document the counter-party says is still being negotiated. CBS News, citing two sources familiar with the diplomatic efforts, said the text is a 'letter of intent or memorandum of understanding' that is 'likely to be signed early next week.' Trump was claiming a signing this weekend. The signing Vance is flying to is for a document that does not yet exist in the form Trump is describing.

The 'deal' is testable in real time on the water. CENTCOM's own figures show the US has disabled 8 ships and redirected 134 since April 13 in the Iran blockade. The most recent strikes — on MT Marivex, MT Settebello, and MT Jalveer — killed three Indian sailors in four days and forced India's foreign ministry to summon the US deputy chief of mission. CENTCOM admitted firing two Hellfire missiles into Jalveer's engine room. That is the operational definition of an active blockade, not a 'deal that reopened the strait.' Iran's Hormuz oversight body said the strait will remain closed 'until further notice.' If the deal is real, AIS feeds would show transit volumes returning toward the pre-conflict ~138 vessels per day baseline. They will not. The same is true of the IRGC's claim of attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, and Kuwait on June 12 — if the war is 'over,' bases are not being hit the same day the deal is announced.

The third contradiction is internal to the administration's own behaviour. Trump announced the deal with rally showmanship — 'the stock market likes the deal' — that treats a diplomatic event as a domestic political product. The pattern of declaring 'deals' the counter-party has not signed is not new. The JCPOA in 2015 took years of multilateral negotiation before any party claimed victory. Korea 1992 took a year of formal talks. A 'very strong memorandum of understanding' is the kind of language that normally appears at the end of a process, not at a campaign rally 24 hours after strikes were 'cancelled.'

Iran's framing of the dispute — 'time and place of signing were speculative' and 'the Trump administration continued to change its position during the talks' — is more specific than the US claim. It names a concrete procedural objection: the US is moving the public narrative faster than the actual negotiations. That is a different kind of contradiction than 'no comment.' It is the counter-party saying: you announced something that does not exist yet.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: Trump's 'ended the war' / 'deal approved' claim is unsupported by the counter-party's official public position, contradicted by the physical evidence on the water, and invalidated by the Israeli government's explicit statement that it is 'not a party to the MOU.' Iran's foreign ministry, the IRGC, the Iranian Army, and the Hormuz oversight body have all contradicted load-bearing elements of the claim within 24 hours. CENTCOM's own operational data — three Indian sailors dead in four days, two Hellfire missiles into a tanker's engine room, US aircraft shooting down Iranian drones the same day as the 'deal' — is incompatible with a war that has ended. The Vance signing trip is for a document that does not yet exist in the form Trump is describing. Until the counter-party signs, the operational posture shifts, and the strait physically reopens, the 'deal' is a public narrative, not a diplomatic fact.
